title: Aggregations Across Joined Tables 📊
description: Combine JOINs with GROUP BY, HAVING, and conditional aggregates to answer complex questions.

slides.title: Real‑World Analysis 📈
slides.content:
# Answer Business Questions with JOINs and Aggregates

Many questions require data from multiple tables, then summarizing. Patterns:
- Total sales by product category (needs products, orders, order_items)
- Average order value per customer
- Customers who bought a specific product along with another

Let’s practice with sample tables.

slides.title: Sample Tables Recap 📋
slides.content:
We’ll use these simplified tables:

**customers**: customer_id, name, city
**orders**: order_id, customer_id, amount

(No order_items/products in this example to keep it simple; we’ll add a third table later if needed.)

slides.title: Question 1: Average Order Amount per City 🏙️
slides.content:
**For each city, what is the average order amount?**

```sql
SELECT c.city, AVG(o.amount) AS avg_amount
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY c.city;
```

Only customers with orders are included (because of INNER JOIN). Use LEFT JOIN if you want to show cities with no orders (avg will be NULL).

slides.title: City Avg Example
slides.codeSnippet:
SELECT c.city, AVG(o.amount) AS avg_amount
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY c.city;

quizData.question: If you GROUP BY a column from table A after JOINing with table B, what rows are grouped?

options.text: The combined result set after the join

quizData.explanation: GROUP BY operates on the result of the FROM/WHERE/JOINs.

slides.title: Question 2: Customers with Total Spending > 400 💰
slides.content:
**List customers whose total spending exceeds 400.**

```sql
SELECT c.name, SUM(o.amount) AS total_spent
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name
HAVING SUM(o.amount) > 400;
```

We group by both customer_id and name (if names are unique, just customer_id is enough).

slides.title: High‑Spending Customers
slides.codeSnippet:
SELECT c.name, SUM(o.amount) AS total
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name
HAVING SUM(o.amount) > 400;

slides.title: Question 3: Customers Who Never Ordered (with Aggregation) 🚫
slides.content:
**Find customers with no orders.** (already seen, but now add count of orders = 0):

```sql
SELECT c.name, COUNT(o.order_id) AS order_count
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name
HAVING COUNT(o.order_id) = 0;
```

`COUNT(o.order_id)` counts only non‑NULL order IDs, so zero means no orders.

quizData.question: Why use COUNT(orders.order_id) instead of COUNT(*) to find customers with no orders?

options.text: COUNT(*) would count the NULL row as 1, giving wrong results

quizData.explanation: After LEFT JOIN, customers with no orders have a single row with NULLs. COUNT(*) counts that row as 1; COUNT(o.order_id) ignores NULL, giving 0.

slides.title: Conditional Aggregates with Joins 🎯
slides.content:
**Count how many orders each customer has in each amount category ('Low' <200, 'High' >=200)**

```sql
SELECT c.name,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN o.amount < 200 THEN 1 END) AS low_orders,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN o.amount >= 200 THEN 1 END) AS high_orders
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name;
```

This gives a summary per customer.

slides.title: Conditional Aggregation with Join
slides.codeSnippet:
SELECT c.name,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN o.amount < 200 THEN 1 END) AS low,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN o.amount >= 200 THEN 1 END) AS high
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name;

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Use GROUP BY with Column Aliases

You can group by column numbers (`GROUP BY 1, 2`) but it's clearer to use names. In some databases, you can group by alias if the alias is defined in the SELECT, but standard SQL doesn't allow that.

slides.title: Final Challenge 🏋️
slides.content:
Given the tables:
- `customers(customer_id, name, city)`
- `orders(order_id, customer_id, amount, order_date)`

Write queries:
1. For each city, show total revenue and number of orders.
2. List customers who have placed at least 2 orders.
3. Show a customer list with a column indicating 'active' (>=1 order) or 'inactive' (0 orders) based on a LEFT JOIN.

Write SQL.

slides.title: JOINs & Aggregations Complete! 🎉
slides.content: You now wield the full power of SQL to query multiple tables and summarize data. Next, we’ll connect pandas with SQL databases.
